items.log_text: Stone basin, knee-deep. Water heated with two bricks pulled from the kiln floor. Hemp cloth worked for an hour — the fibres shrunk laterally and the weave closed up. Nap raised with a dried teasel head. Dense and dull, which is what we wanted.

Nettle twill fulled lighter than the hemp — four minutes less trampling. Wire card raised a short nap that softened the hand considerably. Still scratches against bare skin but is workable with a shirt underneath.

Dog-fur scrim fulled fast — ten minutes before the fibres locked. Had to stop early to prevent felting solid. Nap raised gently. Result is a soft, dense panel. Used as a sleeping mat overlay. The others took notice.

Linen does not full in the same way. After twenty minutes in hot water the cloth is firmer and the weave is set, but no nap forms — linen fibres do not migrate. Useful for stiffening; left it flat-pressed between boards to dry square.

Twill structure fulls more evenly than the plain weave — the diagonal float allows the fibres to migrate uniformly. Teasel raised a longer nap on this one. Cut into two halves: one as a water-pouch sleeve, one stored against winter.

Mixed warp cloth: half hemp, half nettle. The two fibres full at different rates — nettle locks faster, causing a slight warp across the panel width. Blocked and dried under weight. Still usable as a door baffle, which does not require flat.

Honeycomb weave fulled carefully — the raised cell structure would collapse if overworked. Fifteen minutes, minimal trampling, warm rather than hot water. Cells held their relief. Nap raised only at the surface. The air-trapping effect is preserved. First genuinely insulating cloth we have fulled.
